title: Tobacco Trade
timelinePrompt: Shortly after London Town's founding, our first recorded ship, the John and Margaret pulled into port and placed a want ad for tobacco.
timelineCorrectFeedback: That's right! We have well over 200 examples of ships pulling into the port and advertising for local farmers to come in and sell them their tobacco.
closelookingPrompt: What Act listed on the timeline in front of you officially ended the buying and selling of tobacco at London Town?
closelookingAnswers: Tobacco Inspection Act, 1747 | Act for the Advancement of Trade, 1683 | An Act for Advancement of Trade and Erecting Ports and Towns, 1706 | Act Relating to Servants and Slaves, 1715
closelookingFeedback: Yes, although it took several years to be enforced, this law meant that local farmers could no longer sell their tobacco at London Town. The nearest tobacco inspection point was a few miles upriver at Beard's Creek.
closelookingMoreInfo: The Maryland General Assembly hoped that by regulating the trade more heavily, the colony's tobacco reputation would improve.

title: Taverns at London Town
timelinePrompt: On this date, tavern keeper Mehitable Pierpoint went to court. Her husband John Pierpoint had run away, and she was having trouble collecting tavern debts owed that were in his name. She was one of London Town's first tavern keepers.
timelineCorrectFeedback: Right! Mehitable had been running a tavern in the area since the late 1600s, with and without the help of two husbands. She received the court's permission to collect debts on behalf of her truant husband.
closelookingPrompt: What iconic London Town artifact was NOT found at the excavation site of the Rumney/West tavern?
closelookingAnswers: bartmann "bearded man" jug | a mermaid plate | spike bowl (the spike may have held fruit in place for fancy punches) | crystalline glasses
closelookingFeedback: These fairly expensive and unique objects suggest that the tavern offered some upscale dining options. All of these artifacts are on display in the exhibit in the basement of the visitor's center.
closelookingMoreInfo: As London Town was situated along travel and trade routes, there were three or four taverns operating at any given time. The brick tavern is simply the most visually impressive and longlasting.

title: Ferry at the King's Highway
timelinePrompt: Being the official Ferry Master for London Town was a coveted position and allowed the holder a lucrative and steady stream of income. After the death of her husband David Mackelfish, when do you think Alice Macklefish applied for the Ferry Master license?
timelineCorrectFeedback: Correct! The ferry license, while not passed down to family members, was often applied for and kept within a family. Alice applied for it after the death of David, but then her second husband applied for it--and again after the second husband's death she obtains the ferry licens.
closelookingPrompt: A vital part of London Town was its role in the King's Highway--which connected the colonies from Charleston, South Carolina to Boston, Massachusetts. London Town was home to the South River Ferry which allowed people, live stock and supplies to cross to and fro. What lead to the demise of the South River Ferry?
closelookingAnswers: A bridge was built across the South River | The ferry boat sank to the bottom of the South River | No one wanted the ferry license anymore | The invention of cars made the ferry obsolete
closelookingFeedback: That's right! In 1872 a bridge was built about a mile away from original town limits.  This officially ended the site's relevance as a ferry-based transportation hub.
closelookingMoreInfo: Although no trace of the ferry remains today, when you walk along the path that leads from the Carpenter Shop to the William Brown House, the valley on the other side of the fence used to be Scott street, the part of the King's Highway which deadended into the South River Ferry.

title: Slave Trade at London Town
timelinePrompt: London Town is a UNESCO Site of Memory for the Slave Trade. When do you think the first ship carrying enslaved people landed in London Town?
timelineCorrectFeedback: Yes, it is one of four ships that are documented to have bought and sold people at London Town. There are several more slave ships that stopped at London Town to take on tobacco, though whether any additional sales of enslaved people were made is unclear.
closelookingPrompt: On the timeline, in the year 1760, look at the newspaper article detailing the voyage of the Jenny, the last slave ship to come to London Town. What made this journey remarkable?
closelookingAnswers: The crew unshackled and armed several enslaved men to fight off French privateers | There was a successful uprising on board the ship and the crew was overthrown by their captives | The crew kidnapped several people they did not have permission to take, causing a diplomatic incident with Angola | The Jenny carried the ancestor of prominent abolitionist Frederick Douglas
closelookingFeedback: Yes, according to the newspaper article, after the attack was over, the men gave back their weapons and went back into the hold. A lack of any sources from an enslaved person's perspective means that we will never really know exactly how this confrontation went down.
closelookingMoreInfo: London Town historian, Michelle Kerns, has estimated that enslaved people made up almost 60% of London Town's population by 1776.

title: Serving Time: Convict Labor and London Town
timelinePrompt: The Transportation Act of 1718 made forced service in the colonies a common punishment for British convicts. When do you think two convict servants, Thomas Bavin and John Connor escaped and spent a summer terrorizing the South River area as highwaymen?
timelineCorrectFeedback: Yes! After several break-ins and armed robberies, on July 17, 1751 the Maryland Gazette writes that they "have done so many Villainies that the travelling the Road, except in Companies and with Arms, seems unsafe, and People are afraid of coming to Market."
closelookingPrompt: Convict labor was common in Maryland, and in London Town. In 1762, convict servant Mary Jones was taken to court by William Brown for what offense?
closelookingAnswers: getting pregnant while in his service | attempting to run away | failure to go regularly to church |neglect of her duties
closelookingFeedback: Mary Jones was found guilty, and ordered to serve three additional years on top of her seven year sentence, as well as pay a fine. Brown's argument was that, since Mary Jones was part of his household and did not earn a wage from him, the expense and care of the child would fall to him, and thus he deserved compensation. Convict servants were not allowed to marry or start families until their service was up.
closelookingMoreInfo: Brown had four more male convict servants, all of whom ran away at some point during their sentence. Penalties for running away were steep, so it is likely that Brown was a particularly bad person to work for.

title: Maryland State Papers and the William Brown House
timelinePrompt: During the American Revolution, concern over a British invasion of Annapolis prompted the removal of state papers from Annapolis to Upper Marlboro. Brown's tavern is specifically mentioned as a stopping point as the papers made their way inland, with an armed guard. When do you think the papers were here?
timelineCorrectFeedback: Yes. Although British were in the Chesapeake Bay several times over the course of the Revolution, the British always had other targets, and no attempted invasion of Annapolis took place.
closelookingPrompt: William Brown was not the only London Town patriot. One London Town citizen, 21-year old Andrew Ferguson joined a Maryland regiment that would later go on to make a name for themselves at the Battle of Brooklyn as the Maryland 400. What was the name of the regiment?
closelookingAnswers: First Regiment | Fifth Regiment | Second Regiment | Third Regiment
closelookingFeedback: The First Regiment earned its fame by repeatedly charging the British in order to give the rest of Washington's soldier's a chance to retreat. All but twelve were killed or captured, causing Washington to exclaim "Good God! What brave fellows I must this day lose!”
closelookingMoreInfo: Though Andrew Ferguson survived the the day, he ultimately did not survive the war. The will he wrote upon enlisting left everything to his eleven-year old sister Elizabeth.

title: Soldiers by the South River
timelinePrompt: Due to rising fears that Confederate General Jubal Early's campaign would make it to Annapolis, the Union landed a party of sailors "at the lower ferry" and seized all boats that Confederate soldiers could have been used to cross the South River.
timelineCorrectFeedback: Once Jubal Early's campaign was defeated and it was clear Annapolis was under no threat, the vessels were returned.
closelookingPrompt: In total, how many times do you think soldiers were deployed to London Town?
closelookingFeedback: That's right, four!  Twice during the Revolutionary War, once during the War of 1812, and once during the Civil War. No battles were ever fought in the town or on the South River.
closelookingMoreInfo: London Town was a strategic gathering point in times of conflict as its South River Ferry was a part of the King's Highway. The King's Highway was a series of roads and water crossings that connected Charleston, South Carolina to Boston, Massachusetts.

title: From Tavern to Almshouse
timelinePrompt: The brick tavern served as the Anne Arundel County Almshouse from 1823-1965. Underserved and underfunded it came under fire during America's Progressive Era. When do you think it was described as  "filthy," "thoroughly inadequate" and "with no thought to morality"?
timelineCorrectFeedback: That's right. Many such reports in the late 1800s and early 1900s criticized the Almshouse for subparr conditions. This particular complaint comes from the Twenty-Third Report of the Lunacy Commission, and was part of a larger public service movement to get mentally ill people out of almshouses and into specialized facilities.
closelookingPrompt: Look at the physical timeline in front of you and locate the obituary for Almshouse resident Henry Howard. What was his listed profession?
closelookingAnswers: herb doctor | restaurant owner | teacher | factory worker
closelookingFeedback: Yes, which means he was selling medicinal roots and herbal remedies. It is very uncommon for us to have obituary notices for our residents. Though he ended his life in poverty, Howard must have made an impression on his community.
closelookingMoreInfo: Because of the color of his skin, Howard would have lived in the Black Dormitory, which was demolished in 1910 for being run-down and unfit for habitation.

title: London Town and Gardens
timelinePrompt: When London Town became a museum, the four seasons garden was established at the same time. The garden has been used as a test site for reseaching geneticaly modified plants to advance the field of horticulture. When was London Town selected to be a test site for camellias?
timelineCorrectFeedback: Correct! London Town was selected by William Ackerman, a geneticist from the U.S. National Arboretum, to be one of the initial field testing locations for new varieties of camellias.
closelookingPrompt: Before the 1980s, camellias would not survive the colder winters further north than Southern Maryland and Washington D.C. Today, due to the research conducted by Dr. Ackerman and other horticulturalists, camellias can survive to what temperature (°F)?.
closelookingFeedback: Correct! Cold-hardy camellias will thrive in harsh winters in Wisconsin, Ontario, and even Norway!
closelookingMoreInfo: While walking though the gardens, you will be able to find some of the cold-hardy camellias in bloom from October to April. Some of the hybrid verieties include Londontowne Blush, Snow Flurry, Winter's Hope, Winter's Rose, Londontown, and Pink Icicle.

title: London Town Archaeology
timelinePrompt: Archaeologists began to excavate London Town in the 90s, with the founding of the Lost Towns project, an Anne Arundel County intiative that targeted sites with known colonial history. When did archaeologists find the remains of a small child buried at the site of what once was Stephen West's 1720s tobacco warehouse.
timelineCorrectFeedback: That's right. Though the child's identity will forever be a mystery, it is believed that they were part of a family enslaved by Stephen West who lived at London Town sometime from the 1720s to early 1750s. In West African culture, loved ones are often buried underneath the home, with children sometimes being buried underneath the mother's bed. Their remains were reinterred in a ceremony on May 8, 2003.
closelookingPrompt: How many buildings do you think archaeologists found evidence for on site? Do not include the brick tavern in your count, as that has always remained above ground.
closelookingFeedback: Yes, although we have only reconstructed the Tenement House and Carpenter Shop (formerly West's tobacco warehouse and enslaved dwelling), archaeologists also found evidence for an early 1700s tavern and the 19th century Black Dormitory (see more about the Almshouse)
closelookingMoreInfo: Archaeologists still periodically conduct digs on London Town today, and as of 2025, Anne Arundel County's Archaeology Lab is located right next to our visitor's center. Check out their website for ways to volunteer!
